issues.legal_issue: A development authority may transfer its property without a public auction, tender, or advertisement when the applicable rules impose no restriction, condition, or limitation on that transfer.
material_facts: The authority allotted a plot to a newspaper printing and publishing company for establishing an industry and executed a sale deed after the company paid the consideration.
The public interest petition challenged the transfer on the grounds that no auction was held, no tender was called for, and no public advertisement was issued.
The rules cited in the proceedings did not apply to this allotment, and no applicable restriction, condition, or limitation on the transfer had been prescribed.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was not unlawful merely because it was made without an auction, tender, or advertisement; the High Court erred in applying rules that did not govern the allotment.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory power to lease, sell, or otherwise transfer property is not rendered inoperative because rules have not been made, unless the statute makes rules a condition precedent. A power expressed to be subject to rules is exercisable in accordance with rules, if any; where no applicable rules exist, the authority is not thereby precluded from exercising the power. The Court relied on Surinder Singh v. Central Government and Others, Ashok Leyland Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Chairman & MD, BPL Ltd. v. S.P. Gururaja and Others. It distinguished K.R.C.S. Balakrishna Chetty and Sons & Co. v. State of Madras, which concerned an exemption conditional on compliance with prescribed requirements.

predicates.public_interest_challenge: A public interest proceeding challenged a public authority's transfer of land.
predicates.authority_transferred_its_property: A public authority transferred property belonging to it.
predicates.no_applicable_transfer_restrictions: No applicable rule prescribed a restriction, condition, or limitation governing the transfer.

issues.definition: When a public interest proceeding challenges a public authority's transfer of its property and no applicable transfer restrictions exist, the transfer is not invalid solely because no public sale process was used.

issues.legal_issue: An allotment of a plot for an industrial undertaking is not a bulk allotment merely because it is made for industrial use, and the bulk-allotment regime does not govern it on that basis.
material_facts: The authority allotted one plot to a company for an industrial undertaking.

The High Court treated the allotment as a bulk allotment, but the Supreme Court held that the allotment was not bulk and that the land extent must be commensurate with the purpose for which it is allotted.
The transfer was to an industrial undertaking, not a recipient shown to fall within the categories contemplated for bulk allotments.
issues.conclusion: The bulk-allotment provision did not apply to the allotment, and the High Court erred in treating it as a bulk allotment.
issues.legal_principle: The provisions governing ordinary transfers and bulk allotments operate in different fields. The bulk-allotment provision concerns bulk transfers to specified categories of recipients, while the size of an industrial allotment must be assessed in light of its purpose. The Court also relied on Chairman & MD, BPL Ltd. v. S.P. Gururaja and Others when considering an allotment to an industrial undertaking.

predicates.public_interest_challenge: A public interest proceeding challenged a public authority's allotment of land.
predicates.allotment_was_for_industrial_use: The authority allotted land for use by an industrial undertaking.
predicates.allotment_was_not_bulk: The allotment was not a bulk transfer.

issues.definition: When a public interest proceeding challenges a non-bulk allotment made for industrial use, the bulk-allotment regime does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A public interest petition challenging a land allotment may be dismissed for delay when it is brought substantially after the allotment and sale deed.
material_facts: The allotment was made and a sale deed was executed before the public interest petition was filed.
The petition was filed about three years after the allotment and execution of the sale deed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have dismissed the petition on the ground of delay and laches.
issues.legal_principle: A court should consider delay and laches in deciding whether to entertain a public interest petition; on these facts, the delay warranted dismissal.

predicates.public_interest_litigation: The proceeding was a public interest petition challenging a land allotment.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The challenge was brought substantially after the allotment and transfer had taken place.

issues.definition: A public interest petition brought substantially after the challenged allotment and transfer should be dismissed for delay.

issues.legal_issue: When a plea is raised that a public interest litigant has been set up by interested persons, the court should determine that allegation.
material_facts: The company alleged that the public interest petitioner had been set up by interested persons.
The High Court did not appear to have considered that allegation.
issues.conclusion: The court hearing the public interest petition should have determined the allegation when it was raised.
issues.legal_principle: In a public interest proceeding, the court should examine a raised allegation that the petitioner is acting at the instance of interested persons.

predicates.public_interest_litigation: The proceeding was brought as a public interest litigation.
predicates.allegation_petitioner_was_set_up_by_inte: A party alleged that interested persons had arranged for the petitioner to bring the proceeding.

issues.definition: When interested persons are alleged to have arranged for a public interest petitioner to bring the proceeding, the court should determine the petitioner's independence.
